claim: Sex determination is a developmental switch that triggers sex-specific developmental programs.
source: Sex determination is a developmental switch that triggers sex-specific developmental programs.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about sex determination that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Many lineages have evolved sex chromosomes that act as primary signals for sex determination.
source: Many lineages have evolved sex chromosomes that act as primary signals for sex determination.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about sex determination mechanisms across taxa.

claim: Haplodiploidy occurs in ca. 12% of animal species.
source: However, haplodiploidy (males are haploid and females are diploid), which occurs in ca. 12% of animal species, is incompatible with sex chromosomes.
evidence: This is a cited statistic about the prevalence of haplodiploidy.

claim: Haplodiploidy is incompatible with sex chromosomes.
source: However, haplodiploidy (males are haploid and females are diploid), which occurs in ca. 12% of animal species, is incompatible with sex chromosomes.
evidence: This statement is based on logical reasoning about genetic inheritance in haplodiploid systems.

claim: In complementary sex determination (CSD), heterozygosity at a sex determination locus triggers female development, while hemizygosity or homozygosity permits male development.
source: In CSD, heterozygosity at a sex determination locus triggers female development, while hemizygosity or homozygosity permits male development.
evidence: This is a definition of the CSD mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: CSD loci have been mapped in honeybees and two ant species.
source: CSD loci have been mapped in honeybees and two ant species, but we know little about their evolutionary history.
evidence: This statement refers to prior research on CSD loci mapping.

claim: A 46 kb candidate CSD locus was identified in Ooceraea biroi at which all females are heterozygous, but most diploid males are homozygous for either allele.
source: We identified a 46 kb candidate CSD locus at which all females are heterozygous, but most diploid males are homozygous for either allele.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic mapping study presented in the manuscript.

claim: The candidate CSD locus has more alleles than most other loci, resulting in a peak of nucleotide diversity.
source: As expected for CSD loci, the candidate locus has more alleles than most other loci, resulting in a peak of nucleotide diversity.
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide diversity analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The peak of nucleotide diversity at the candidate CSD locus negligibly affects the amino acid sequences of protein-coding genes.
source: This peak negligibly affects the amino acid sequences of protein-coding genes, suggesting that heterozygosity of a non-coding genomic sequence triggers female development.
evidence: This is based on analysis of sequence variation at the locus.

claim: Heterozygosity of a non-coding genomic sequence triggers female development in O. biroi.
source: This peak negligibly affects the amino acid sequences of protein-coding genes, suggesting that heterozygosity of a non-coding genomic sequence triggers female development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nucleotide diversity does not affect protein-coding sequences.

claim: The O. biroi CSD locus is distinct from the CSD locus in honeybees.
source: This locus is distinct from the CSD locus in honeybees but homologous to a CSD locus mapped in two distantly related ant species, implying that this molecular mechanism has been conserved since a common ancestor that lived approximately 112 million years ago.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis showing lack of homology to honeybee CSD.

claim: The O. biroi CSD locus is homologous to a CSD locus mapped in two distantly related ant species.
source: This locus is distinct from the CSD locus in honeybees but homologous to a CSD locus mapped in two distantly related ant species, implying that this molecular mechanism has been conserved since a common ancestor that lived approximately 112 million years ago.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis showing homology to V. emeryi and L. humile CSD loci.

claim: The CSD molecular mechanism has been conserved since a common ancestor that lived approximately 112 million years ago.
source: This locus is distinct from the CSD locus in honeybees but homologous to a CSD locus mapped in two distantly related ant species, implying that this molecular mechanism has been conserved since a common ancestor that lived approximately 112 million years ago.
evidence: This is inferred from the homology of the locus across distantly related ant species and phylogenetic dating.

claim: Downstream transcription factors that encode sexual identity are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Although the downstream transcription factors are evolutionarily conserved, primary sex determination signals are evolutionarily labile and comprise a diverse range of environmental and genetic mechanisms (Bachtrog et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bachtrog et al., 2014.

claim: Primary sex determination signals are evolutionarily labile and comprise a diverse range of environmental and genetic mechanisms.
source: Although the downstream transcription factors are evolutionarily conserved, primary sex determination signals are evolutionarily labile and comprise a diverse range of environmental and genetic mechanisms (Bachtrog et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bachtrog et al., 2014.

claim: An estimated 12% of animal species are haplodiploid, including ants.
source: Genetically encoded primary signals (sex-determining genes or chromosomes) are usually found in only one sex. Such systems do not work in haplodiploid taxa (an estimated 12% of animal species, including ants; Normark, 2003), where any allele on any homologous chromosome can be transmitted from diploid females to their haploid male sons, and all alleles experience selection to be viably transmitted from both sexes (Whiting, 1935).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Normark, 2003.

claim: In haplodiploid taxa, any allele on any homologous chromosome can be transmitted from diploid females to their haploid male sons.
source: Such systems do not work in haplodiploid taxa (an estimated 12% of animal species, including ants; Normark, 2003), where any allele on any homologous chromosome can be transmitted from diploid females to their haploid male sons, and all alleles experience selection to be viably transmitted from both sexes (Whiting, 1935).
evidence: This is based on the genetic logic of haplodiploidy and supported by citation to Whiting, 1935.

claim: Some parasitoid wasps use a sex determination mechanism involving maternal imprinting.
source: Some parasitoid wasps use a mechanism involving maternal imprinting (Verhulst et al., 2010; Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Verhulst et al., 2010 and Zou et al., 2020.

claim: In many Hymenoptera, inbred crosses produce diploid males.
source: However, in many Hymenoptera, inbred crosses produce diploid males, which led to the hypothesis that female development is triggered by heterozygosity as a proxy for diploidy (Whiting, 1933; Whiting, 1943).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Whiting, 1933 and Whiting, 1943.

claim: Under CSD, diploid males produce diploid sperm and are functionally sterile.
source: Under CSD, diploid males produce diploid sperm and, therefore, are functionally sterile (van Wilgenburg et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Wilgenburg et al., 2006.

claim: There is selection against homozygosity at CSD loci at the population level, often meaning obligatory avoidance of inbreeding.
source: This has several evolutionary consequences (Cook and Crozier, 1995); at the population level, there is selection against homozygosity, often meaning obligatory avoidance of inbreeding (Page, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook and Crozier, 1995 and Page, 1980.

claim: There is negative frequency-dependent (balancing) selection on CSD loci, resulting in the co-occurrence of many alleles at similar frequencies within populations.
source: At the gene level, there is negative frequency-dependent (balancing) selection on CSD loci, resulting in the co-occurrence of many alleles at similar frequencies within populations (Laidlaw et al., 1956).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laidlaw et al., 1956.

claim: CSD was demonstrated in the honeybee Apis mellifera in 2003.
source: Having been a favored hypothesis for more than half a century, CSD was demonstrated in the honeybee Apis mellifera in 2003 (Beye et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beye et al., 2003.

claim: In A. mellifera, biallelic heteromers of the protein encoded by the complementary sex determiner (csd) gene trigger female development, whereas monoallelic homomers permit male development.
source: In A. mellifera, biallelic heteromers of the protein encoded by the complementary sex determiner (csd) gene trigger female development, whereas monoallelic homomers permit male development (Beye et al., 2003; Beye et al., 2013; Otte et al., 2023; Seiler and Beye, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beye et al., 2003; Beye et al., 2013; Otte et al., 2023; Seiler and Beye, 2024.

claim: The Csd protein sex-specifically splices the closely linked splicing factor feminizer (fem) in A. mellifera.
source: The Csd protein sex-specifically splices the closely linked splicing factor feminizer (fem) (the honeybee version of transformer [tra] in Drosophila and other insects), which in turn leads to the production of sex-specific isoforms of doublesex (dsx), a transcription factor that regulates sex-specific development (Hasselmann et al., 2008; Gempe et al., 2009; Verhulst et al., 2010; Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hasselmann et al., 2008; Gempe et al., 2009; Verhulst et al., 2010; Zou et al., 2020.

claim: The honeybee csd gene is a paralog of fem.
source: Intriguingly, csd is a paralog of fem.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the evolutionary relationship between these genes.

claim: Many csd alleles are held at similar frequencies in A. mellifera.
source: Following the prediction that CSD loci should evolve under balancing selection, many csd alleles are held at similar frequencies, and the locus bears signatures of adaptive evolution (Hasselmann and Beye, 2004), with amino acid-level heterozygosity in certain protein domains required for female development (Otte et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hasselmann and Beye, 2004 and Otte et al., 2023.

claim: The A. mellifera csd locus bears signatures of adaptive evolution.
source: Following the prediction that CSD loci should evolve under balancing selection, many csd alleles are held at similar frequencies, and the locus bears signatures of adaptive evolution (Hasselmann and Beye, 2004), with amino acid-level heterozygosity in certain protein domains required for female development (Otte et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hasselmann and Beye, 2004.

claim: Amino acid-level heterozygosity in certain protein domains of A. mellifera Csd is required for female development.
source: Following the prediction that CSD loci should evolve under balancing selection, many csd alleles are held at similar frequencies, and the locus bears signatures of adaptive evolution (Hasselmann and Beye, 2004), with amino acid-level heterozygosity in certain protein domains required for female development (Otte et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Otte et al., 2023.

claim: A genetic mapping study in the wasp Lysiphlebus fabarum identified at least one and as many as four candidate sex determination loci.
source: A recent genetic mapping study in the wasp Lysiphlebus fabarum identified at least one and as many as four candidate sex determination loci (Matthey-Doret et al., 2019) (the multi-locus extension of the CSD hypothesis proposes that heterozygosity at any of multiple sex determination loci is sufficient to trigger female development [Crozier, 1971; Figure 1b]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matthey-Doret et al., 2019.

claim: In the ant Vollenhovia emeryi, a mapping study found two sex determination QTL.
source: In the ant Vollenhovia emeryi, a mapping study found two sex determination QTL (Miyakawa and Mikheyev, 2015), with follow-up work suggesting that these function as a multi-locus CSD system (Miyakawa and Miyakawa, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miyakawa and Mikheyev, 2015 and Miyakawa and Miyakawa, 2023.

claim: One of the V. emeryi CSD QTL (V.emeryiCsdQTL1) contains two closely linked tra homologs.
source: One of these QTL (V.emeryiCsdQTL1) contains two closely linked tra homologs, reminiscent of the locus containing csd and fem in A. mellifera.
evidence: This is based on the genetic mapping data from V. emeryi.

claim: A sex determination locus was identified in the Argentine ant, Linepithema humile.
source: Recently, a sex determination locus was identified in the Argentine ant, Linepithema humile (Pan et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: In L. humile, all pairwise heterozygous combinations of the seven identified alleles were found in females, whereas diploid males were invariably homozygous for one of the seven alleles.
source: Consistent with CSD, all pairwise heterozygous combinations of the seven identified alleles were found in females, whereas diploid males were invariably homozygous for one of the seven alleles.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: The L. humile CSD alleles occurred at roughly equal frequencies within populations, suggesting evolution under balancing selection.
source: Moreover, these alleles occurred at roughly equal frequencies within populations, suggesting evolution under balancing selection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: The L. humile CSD locus is located within a noncoding genomic region tightly linked to ant noncoding transformer splicing regulator (ANTSR), a long noncoding RNA (lncRNA).
source: The mapped locus is located within a noncoding genomic region tightly linked to ant noncoding transformer splicing regulator (ANTSR), a long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) with previously uncharacterized function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: ANTSR knockdown in female-destined embryos leads to male-specific splicing of tra in L. humile.
source: ANTSR knockdown in female-destined embryos leads to male-specific splicing of tra, suggesting that this lncRNA transduces the primary sex determination signal encoded by the heterozygosity (or hemi- or homozygosity) of the linked noncoding region (Pan et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: The synteny of the L. humile CSD region (including the presence of a lncRNA putatively homologous to ANTSR) is conserved across the ants, bees, and vespoid wasps.
source: Because the synteny of this region (including the presence of a lncRNA putatively homologous to ANTSR) is conserved across the ants, bees, and vespoid wasps, it was suggested that this sex determination locus may be deeply conserved among the Aculeata (Pan et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: Diploid males occur sporadically in O. biroi, suggesting that they might employ CSD.
source: Diploid males occur sporadically in this species, suggesting that, like other ants, they might employ CSD (Kronauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kronauer et al., 2012.

claim: O. biroi reproduces via a mode of parthenogenesis in which two haploid nuclei from a single meiosis fuse to produce diploid offspring (central fusion automixis).
source: O. biroi reproduces via a mode of parthenogenesis in which two haploid nuclei from a single meiosis fuse to produce diploid offspring (central fusion automixis) (Oxley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oxley et al., 2014.

claim: Heterozygosity is maintained with high fidelity in O. biroi despite meiotic crossover recombination.
source: Although heterozygosity is maintained with high fidelity despite meiotic crossover recombination (Lacy et al., 2024), losses of heterozygosity occur occasionally, probably due to the inheritance of one recombined and one non-recombined version of a homologous chromosome (Kronauer et al., 2012; Oxley et al., 2014; Trible et al., 2023; Lacy et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lacy et al., 2024.

claim: Losses of heterozygosity occur occasionally in O. biroi, probably due to the inheritance of one recombined and one non-recombined version of a homologous chromosome.
source: Although heterozygosity is maintained with high fidelity despite meiotic crossover recombination (Lacy et al., 2024), losses of heterozygosity occur occasionally, probably due to the inheritance of one recombined and one non-recombined version of a homologous chromosome (Kronauer et al., 2012; Oxley et al., 2014; Trible et al., 2023; Lacy et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kronauer et al., 2012; Oxley et al., 2014; Trible et al., 2023; Lacy et al., 2024.

claim: Sixteen diploid males were sequenced and compared with 19 previously sequenced genomes of diploid females.
source: We then sequenced the genomes of 16 diploid males and compared them with 19 previously sequenced genomes of diploid females (Trible et al., 2023; Lacy et al., 2024) (descriptions and metadata for all genomes sequenced in this study are in Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample sizes used in the study.

claim: A peak of the CSD index was found on chromosome 4, which deviated significantly from the null distribution of CSD index values.
source: We found a peak of the CSD index on chromosome 4, which deviated significantly from the null distribution of CSD index values (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic mapping analysis, supported by Figure 2a.

claim: At the CSD index peak, homozygosity levels differed significantly between males and females.
source: At this peak, homozygosity levels differed significantly between males and females (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Eleven out of 16 sequenced diploid males bore segmental losses of heterozygosity on chromosome 4.
source: Eleven out of 16 sequenced diploid males bore segmental losses of heterozygosity on chromosome 4 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the genomic data, illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: The intersection of LOH segments comprised a 46 kb peak at which all females were heterozygous, and most (11 out of 16) diploid males were homozygous.
source: The intersection of these LOH segments comprised a 46 kb peak at which all females were heterozygous, and most (11 out of 16) diploid males were homozygous.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of LOH segments.

claim: O. biroi diploid males were homozygous for either allele at the 46 kb region on chromosome 4.
source: Consistently, O. biroi diploid males were homozygous for either allele at the 46 kb region on chromosome 4 (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Runs of homozygosity in diploid males were not accompanied by changes in copy number.
source: To distinguish between these two scenarios, we analyzed read depth and found that runs of homozygosity were not accompanied by changes in copy number (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on read depth analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Diploid males arise when rare losses of heterozygosity, which result from crossover recombination during meiosis, span the CSD locus.
source: This implies that diploid males arise when rare losses of heterozygosity, which result from crossover recombination during meiosis, span the CSD locus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LOH regions are copy-neutral.

claim: Five of the 16 diploid males were not homozygous in the 46 kb CSD region.
source: Surprisingly, 5 of the 16 diploid males were not homozygous in this 46 kb region.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the genomic data.

claim: No mutations or losses of heterozygosity in genes with annotated sex-determining functions were found in the five diploid males that retained heterozygosity at the CSD locus.
source: We therefore inspected all unique mutations and losses of heterozygosity in these five diploid males, but did not find any in genes with annotated sex-determining functions (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of mutations and LOH in these individuals.

claim: No homology was found between the genes within the O. biroi CSD index peak and any of the genes within the putative L. fabarum CSD loci.
source: We found no homology between the genes within the O. biroi CSD index peak and any of the genes within the putative L. fabarum CSD loci (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Homology to V.emeryiCsdQTL2 was found scattered across one arm of O. biroi chromosome 4, including the 46 kb CSD index peak.
source: Homology to V.emeryiCsdQTL2 was scattered across one arm of O. biroi chromosome 4, including the 46 kb CSD index peak, and homology to the L. humile CSD locus mapped within the O. biroi CSD index peak (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Homology to the L. humile CSD locus mapped within the O. biroi CSD index peak.
source: Homology to V.emeryiCsdQTL2 was scattered across one arm of O. biroi chromosome 4, including the 46 kb CSD index peak, and homology to the L. humile CSD locus mapped within the O. biroi CSD index peak (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The O. biroi CSD index peak contains four protein-coding genes that are also present in V.emeryiCsdQTL2, including HCF, COPA, an uncharacterized gene, and CRELD2.
source: The O. biroi CSD index peak contains four protein-coding genes that are also present in V.emeryiCsdQTL2, including HCF, COPA, an uncharacterized gene, and CRELD2.
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and comparative analysis.

claim: The candidate CSD region in O. biroi includes a large stretch of sequence with no annotated genes downstream of an uncharacterized lncRNA.
source: Notably, the candidate CSD region in O. biroi also includes a large stretch of sequence with no annotated genes downstream of an uncharacterized lncRNA.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: All females from all six clonal lines (including 26 diploid females from clonal line B) were heterozygous at the CSD index peak.
source: All females from all six clonal lines (including 26 diploid females from clonal line B) were heterozygous at the CSD index peak, consistent with its putative role as a CSD locus in all O. biroi (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of multiple clonal lines, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Seven haplotypes (or 'alleles') were identified in the five clonal lines for which at least one haploid male genome was sequenced (including the reference genome haplotype).
source: In addition to the haplotype found in the reference genome, we identified six haplotypes (or 'alleles') in the five clonal lines for which we sequenced at least one haploid male genome (Figure 4c, Table 2).
evidence: This is based on de novo assembly and analysis of haploid male genomes, shown in Figure 4c and Table 2.

claim: None of the protein-coding genes within the CSD index peak contained substantial heterozygosity that affected amino acid identity.
source: Within this region, none of the protein-coding genes contained substantial heterozygosity that affected amino acid identity (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sequence variation in protein-coding genes.

claim: Many genes were differentially expressed between males and females (24.6% of expressed genes).
source: Many genes were differentially expressed between males and females (24.6% of expressed genes) or had one or more differentially used exons, including four genes near the CSD index peak (LOC105285605, LOC105283850, LOC105283849, and LOC105283844) (Supplementary file 10 and Supplementary file 11, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary files 10 and 11.

claim: Four genes near the CSD index peak (LOC105285605, LOC105283850, LOC105283849, and LOC105283844) had one or more differentially used exons.
source: Many genes were differentially expressed between males and females (24.6% of expressed genes) or had one or more differentially used exons, including four genes near the CSD index peak (LOC105285605, LOC105283850, LOC105283849, and LOC105283844) (Supplementary file 10 and Supplementary file 11, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on differential exon usage analysis shown in Supplementary files 10 and 11.

claim: None of the differentially expressed genes or genes with differentially used exons overlapped with the region of elevated genetic diversity.
source: However, none of these overlapped with the region of elevated genetic diversity.
evidence: This is based on comparison of differential expression results with the nucleotide diversity peak.

claim: From clonal line A, 22 out of 114 males were diploid, whereas all 78 males genotyped from clonal line B were haploid.
source: In total, from clonal line A, 22 out of 114 males were diploid, whereas all 78 males genotyped from clonal line B were haploid (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on genotyping data shown in Table 3.

claim: The disparity in diploid male production between clonal lines A and B is statistically significant (χ²=15.4, df = 1, p<0.0001).
source: This disparity is statistically significant (χ²=15.4, df = 1, p<0.0001), suggesting that the two clonal lines differ in their propensity to produce diploid males.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the diploid male production data.

claim: No additional candidate CSD loci were identified in the mapping study beyond the chromosome 4 locus.
source: However, we identified no additional candidate loci in our mapping study, and other possibilities are equally likely, including that clonal line A is more prone to loss of heterozygosity, or is more permissive to diploid male development than other clonal lines.
evidence: This is based on the results of the genome-wide mapping analysis.

claim: No sex determination locus with homology to the V. emeryi QTL1 was found in L. humile.
source: However, we did not find a CSD index peak on chromosome 2, and no sex determination locus with homology to the V. emeryi QTL was found in L. humile (Pan et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2024.

claim: Clonal lines A and C are homozygous in a region homologous to a portion of V.emeryiQTL1.
source: Intriguingly, while clonal lines B, D, I, and M retain heterozygosity at all sites with homology to V.emeryiQTL1 (Figure 5c), clonal lines A and C are homozygous in a region homologous to a portion of V.emeryiQTL1.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: All clonal lines are heterozygous in the region containing O. biroi's tra ortholog.
source: We also note that all clonal lines are heterozygous in the region containing O. biroi's tra ortholog (Figure 5c), and that this gene is sex-specifically spliced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), similar to tra homologs in other Holometabola (Hasselmann et al., 2008; Miyakawa and Miyakawa, 2023).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 5c and splicing analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: O. biroi tra is sex-specifically spliced.
source: We also note that all clonal lines are heterozygous in the region containing O. biroi's tra ortholog (Figure 5c), and that this gene is sex-specifically spliced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), similar to tra homologs in other Holometabola (Hasselmann et al., 2008; Miyakawa and Miyakawa, 2023).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tra-like gene in V. emeryi is not sex-specifically spliced, like A. mellifera csd.
source: This contrasts with the tra-like gene in V. emeryi, which, like A. mellifera csd, is not sex-specifically spliced (Miyakawa and Miyakawa, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miyakawa and Miyakawa, 2023.

claim: The mapped locus corresponds to a region with high genetic diversity, following the expectation that CSD loci should evolve under balancing selection.
source: We then showed that this locus is homologous to a sex determination locus found in two other ant species—V. emeryi and L. humile (Figure 3), suggesting that this mechanism of sex determination may be conserved among formicoid ants. By sequencing whole genomes of haploid males and diploid females from other clonal lines of O. biroi, we showed that the mapped locus corresponds to a region with high genetic diversity, following the expectation that CSD loci should evolve under balancing selection (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: O. biroi is one of three ant species for which heterozygosity-dependent female development has been demonstrated at mapped CSD loci.
source: Along with L. humile (Pan et al., 2024) and V. emeryi (Miyakawa and Mikheyev, 2015), O. biroi is now one of three ant species for which heterozygosity-dependent female development has been demonstrated at mapped CSD loci.
evidence: This is based on the results of this study and prior work cited.

claim: The O. biroi CSD locus colocalizes with a peak of nucleotide diversity.
source: As was found in L. humile, this locus colocalizes with a peak of nucleotide diversity (Figure 4), with seven alleles found among five clonal lines (Figure 4c, Table 2), consistent with the expectation that CSD loci should harbor many alleles due to evolution under balancing selection.
evidence: This is based on nucleotide diversity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The role of the CSD locus in sex determination evolved before the divergence of the Dorylinae from the other formicoid ants roughly 112 million years ago.
source: This implies that the role of this locus in CSD evolved before the divergence of the Dorylinae from the other formicoid ants roughly 112 million years ago (Borowiec et al., 2025).
evidence: This is inferred from the homology of the locus across distantly related ant species and phylogenetic dating.

claim: The mode of CSD in O. biroi is not homologous to the system in A. mellifera mediated by the transformer homologs csd and fem.
source: We did not find a peak of the CSD index at the O. biroi tra homolog (Figure 5), indicating that, as in L. humile, the mode of CSD is not homologous to the system in A. mellifera mediated by the transformer homologs csd and fem.
evidence: This is based on the mapping results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Diploid males were only produced in clonal line A, even though many males were collected from other clonal lines.
source: Curiously, diploid males were only produced in clonal line A, even though many males were collected from other clonal lines (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on genotyping data shown in Table 3.

claim: Clonal line A is ancestrally homozygous for a portion of the region homologous to the second V. emeryi QTL.
source: Clonal line A is ancestrally homozygous for a portion of the region homologous to the second V. emeryi QTL, although it retains heterozygosity in the region overlapping tra (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The region homologous to V. emeryi QTL1 lacks elevated nucleotide diversity and functional heterozygosity in O. biroi.
source: However, this region lacks elevated genetic diversity and functional heterozygosity, making it a poor candidate for a second, undetected, CSD locus.
evidence: This is based on nucleotide diversity analysis and sequence analysis.

claim: Five of the 16 sequenced diploid males retained heterozygosity at the mapped CSD locus.
source: Another peculiarity of our study is that 5 of the 16 sequenced diploid males retained heterozygosity at the mapped CSD locus.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the genomic data.

claim: Certain allelic combinations of A. mellifera csd trigger female development with incomplete penetrance.
source: Certain allelic combinations of A. mellifera csd trigger female development with incomplete penetrance (Beye et al., 2013), and the allelic combination found in clonal line A might similarly be permissive to occasional male development.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beye et al., 2013.

claim: In O. biroi, genetically encoded diploid males only result from loss of heterozygosity, which is rare.
source: This is because genetically encoded diploid males only result from loss of heterozygosity, which is rare in O. biroi (Oxley et al., 2014; Lacy et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oxley et al., 2014 and Lacy et al., 2024.

claim: In sexually reproducing populations, diploid males homozygous for sex determination loci will arise much more frequently due to matings between individuals that share an allele at the sex determination locus.
source: By contrast, in sexually reproducing populations, diploid males homozygous for sex determination loci will arise much more frequently due to matings between individuals that share an allele at the sex determination locus (this effect is exacerbated in invasive species like L. humile that have undergone recent genetic bottlenecks).
evidence: This is based on logical reasoning about the genetics of sexual reproduction and CSD.

claim: Species with CSD should obligatorily outbreed or have other mechanisms of maintaining heterozygosity due to the high fitness cost of producing sterile diploid males.
source: Due to the high fitness cost of producing sterile diploid males, species with CSD should obligatorily outbreed or have other mechanisms of maintaining heterozygosity (van Wilgenburg et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Wilgenburg et al., 2006.

claim: Most diploid males resulted from rare crossover-associated losses of heterozygosity that spanned the putative CSD locus.

claim: In many taxa, asexual lineages reproduce via mechanisms that lead to complete homozygosity in a single generation.
source: Intriguingly, in many taxa, asexual lineages reproduce via mechanisms that lead to complete homozygosity in a single generation (Suomalainen et al., 1987; Ma and Schwander, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suomalainen et al., 1987 and Ma and Schwander, 2017.

claim: Among the social Hymenoptera (and other Vespoids), the known modes of asexual reproduction all maintain at least some heterozygosity.

claim: Asexual reproduction with high rates of heterozygosity loss would incur a steep fitness penalty in taxa with CSD due to the production of sterile diploid males.
